definition: Co-occurrence network, sometimes referred to as a semantic network, is a method to analyze text that includes a graphic visualization of potential relationships between people, organizations, concepts, biological organisms like bacteria or other entities represented within written material.
details: The generation and visualization of co-occurrence networks has become practical with the advent of electronically stored text compliant to text mining. By way of definition, co-occurrence networks are the collective interconnection of terms based on their paired presence within a specified unit of text. Networks are generated by connecting pairs of terms using a set of criteria defining co-occurrence. For example, terms A and B may be said to “co-occur” if they both appear in a particular article. Another article may contain terms B and C. Linking A to B and B to C creates a co-occurrence network of these three terms. Rules to define co-occurrence within a text corpus can be set according to desired criteria. For example, a more stringent criteria for co-occurrence may require a pair of terms to appear in the same sentence. Co-occurrence networks were found to be particularly useful to analyze large text and big data, when identifying the main themes and topics (such as in a large number of social media posts), revealing biases in the text (such as biases in news coverage), or even mapping an entire research field.

explainer.lead: A co-occurrence network turns repeated appearances of terms in text into a map of connections. It helps reveal themes, possible biases, and relationships across collections too large to read closely.

tiers.eli5: Imagine drawing a line between two words whenever they show up in the same school assignment. If one assignment mentions dogs and parks, and another mentions parks and balls, you get a chain from dogs to parks to balls. Looking at many lines can show which ideas gather together.
tiers.practitioner: Choose a text unit and co-occurrence rule, then connect each qualifying pair of terms to build the network. Article-level links capture broad associations, while requiring terms to share a sentence is more stringent. The chosen rule strongly shapes the result, and a connection indicates paired presence rather than a confirmed real-world relationship.
tiers.paperLevel: For a text corpus divided into units U, define G = (V, E), where V contains terms and (A, B) belongs to E when A and B satisfy the chosen paired-presence criterion within a unit. Possible units include an article or a sentence. The network represents potential relationships under that criterion; it does not by itself establish their meaning, direction, or causation.

explainer.example: If one article contains terms A and B, link A to B. If another contains B and C, link B to C; the resulting network is A—B—C, with no direct A—C link unless those terms also co-occur.

usedIn.detail: Revealing possible biases in news coverage through patterns of connected terms.

usedIn.name: Research-field mapping
usedIn.detail: Using connections across written material to map an entire research field.

explainer.intuition: Terms that repeatedly appear together can be drawn as connected points, forming a map of how ideas, people, organizations, or other entities occur together in writing. The meaning of each connection depends on the rule used to create it.
howItWorks: Divide the text into units such as articles or sentences, then connect pairs of terms that appear together under the chosen criterion. Combining these pairwise links produces the network, which can be visualized and examined for themes and other patterns.
explainer.whyItMatters: Electronically stored text and text mining make these networks practical for large text collections and big data. They provide a visual way to identify prominent topics, expose possible biases, and map relationships across a research field.
misconceptions: A link does not prove causation.
Co-occurrence can be defined at article or sentence level.
Different linking rules can produce different networks.
Connections represent potential relationships, not confirmed ones.
